links.note: 621 says to laugh when trouble comes (இடுக்கண் வருங்கால் நகுக), since nothing presses it back as well. 774 shows a warrior who, having thrown his spear at an elephant, pulls out the one lodged in his own body and laughs (மெய்வேல் பறியா நகும்). The battlefield verse acts out the advice of 621: the laugh comes at the moment of injury, and the injury is turned to use.

Both verses turn on the same play of உள்ளம் (mind) and உள்ளுதல் (to think): in 622 a flood of suffering perishes when the wise person thinks with the mind (உள்ளத்தின் உள்ளக் கெடும்), and in 309 all one has thought of is gained if one does not think anger in the mind (உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளான் வெகுளி எனின்). Read together they make a single act of thought decide the outcome, once by what is thought and once by what is left unthought.

429 says those whose understanding guards against what is coming (எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்) have no affliction that arrives to shake them; 622 says that for the person of understanding (அறிவுடையான்) even a flood of suffering already present is ended by thinking. The pair gives understanding two jobs, forestalling trouble and dissolving the trouble that came anyway, which Parimelazhagar takes in 622 to be trouble from fate.

623 says those who do not suffer at suffering (இடும்பைக்கு இடும்பை படாஅதவர்) make suffering itself suffer; Parimelazhagar places this in the middle of an undertaking. 261 makes bearing the pain that comes (உற்றநோய் நோன்றல்) half of the form of தவம். The same endurance is a means to finishing work in one book and the definition of austerity in the other.

624 likens the person who pulls through every obstruction to a draught ox (மடுத்தவாயெல்லாம் பகடன்னான்) and says the trouble he meets is itself troubled. 597 says the strong do not give way where things break down (சிதைவிடத்து ஒல்கார்), like an elephant standing firm under arrows. Both make the same claim through a working or fighting animal; the ox adds forward motion to the elephant's holding of ground.

624 says trouble is troubled by one who hauls on like an ox through every blocked place. 620 carries the claim to its limit: those who labour on without flagging (தாழாது உஞற்றுபவர்) see the back even of fate (ஊழையும் உப்பக்கம் காண்பர்). What 624 says of obstacles in the road, 620 says of the power behind them.

625 says that though troubles come stacked (அடுக்கி வரினும்), those of one who is not undone (அழிவிலான்) are themselves in trouble. 989 says those called the shore of worth do not shift even if the age shifts (ஊழி பெயரினும் தாம் பெயரார்). Both define a person by not moving under pressure, one in the chapter on a king's undertakings and one in the chapter on character.

1045 states as plain fact that within the one suffering called poverty many sufferings arrive and settle (பல்குரைத் துன்பங்கள் சென்று படும்), and offers no remedy. 625 addresses exactly such piling up (அடுக்கி வரினும்) and says it fails against one who is not undone. Set side by side, 625's confidence is conditional on the person, while 1045 describes what the stacking is like for those in want.

626 asks whether those who never clutched at wealth saying 'we have got it' (பெற்றேமென்று ஓம்புதல் தேற்றாதவர்) would grieve saying 'we have lost it'. 379 asks why those who see good things as good when they come grieve when the opposite comes (அல்லற் படுவது எவன்). Both use the same verb of grieving in a rhetorical question and locate grief at loss in one's attitude at the time of gain; 379 puts it under fate, 626 under steadiness in trouble.

626 says those who did not cling when they had wealth will not lament 'அற்றேம்'. 593 says those who hold steady energy as their cash in hand (ஊக்கம் ஒருவந்தம் கைத்துடையார்) do not fret 'ஆக்கம் இழந்தேம்'. Both quote the cry of loss in order to deny it, but for different reasons: in 626 the wealth was never held tightly, in 593 something else is counted as the real holding.

341 gives the renouncer's rule: from whatever one has moved away, from that one has no pain (யாதனின் நீங்கியான் நோதல் அதனின் இலன்). 626 applies a milder version within worldly life: one need not give wealth up, only not hoard it (ஓம்புதல் தேற்றாதவர்), to be free of grief at its loss.

627 says the high-minded know the body is a target for suffering (இலக்கம் உடம்பு இடும்பைக்கு) and so do not take trouble as distress. 1029 asks whether the body of one who shields his family from harm is a vessel for suffering alone (இடும்பைக்கே கொள்கலம் கொல்லோ ... உடம்பு). The two share the figure of the body as the place where இடும்பை lands; 627 makes it a general truth to be accepted, 1029 a question raised by one person's burden.

Both verses open with the same words, இன்பம் விழையான் (one who does not desire pleasure). In 628 he also holds that suffering is natural (இடும்பை இயல்பென்பான்) and so does not come to pain; in 615 he desires the work instead (வினை விழைவான்) and becomes a pillar that wipes away his kin's sorrow. 615 extends the benefit of 628 from the person himself to those who depend on him.

628 says one who does not desire pleasure and takes suffering as natural does not come to pain (துன்பம் உறுதல் இலன்). 368 says those without craving have no sorrow (அவா இல்லார்க்கு இல்லாகும் துன்பம்), and where craving exists sorrow keeps coming. The logic that absence of wanting removes pain appears in the renunciation chapters as a path to release and here as equipment for a person at work in the world.

629 says one who does not crave pleasure in the midst of pleasure does not suffer in the midst of pain. 115 says loss and increase are both part of life and that not letting the heart bend (நெஞ்சத்துக் கோடாமை) is the ornament of the worthy. Both ask for the same evenness across good and bad turns; 115 treats it as fairness of mind, 629 as protection against pain.

629 makes freedom from pain depend on not desiring pleasure when it is present (இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் விழையாதான்). 4 describes the Lord as one without wanting or not-wanting (வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான்) and says those who reach his feet never have இடும்பை. The same link between having no pull toward or away from things and having no suffering appears as a divine attribute in Book 1 and as a human discipline here.

669 says to do with resolve the deed that yields joy even though pain comes thick at first (துன்பம் உறவரினும் ... இன்பம் பயக்கும் வினை): pain now, joy later. 630 goes a step further and has the person take the pain itself as joy (இன்னாமை இன்பம் எனக்கொளின்). Parimelazhagar reads the pain in both as the strain of effort.

630 says that taking what hurts as pleasure brings a distinction (சிறப்பு) even enemies esteem. 267 says that for those able to endure, pain as it burns makes them shine like gold in fire (துன்பம் சுடச்சுட ... ஒளிவிடும்). In both, pain rightly borne produces visible excellence; 267 says it of austerity, 630 of worldly effort.

630 measures the reward by the enemy: a distinction one's foes desire or esteem (ஒன்னார் விழையும் சிறப்பு). 810 uses the same measure with the same verb: those who do not depart from their nature toward old friends are wanted even by those who do not want them (விழையார் விழையப்படுப). Each verse marks an unusual constancy, under pain or toward friends who have erred, by saying that even the hostile regard it.

The two verses end with the same formula, 'அந்நலம்/பிறநலம் யா/எந்நலத்து உள்ளதூஉம் அன்று', used in opposite directions. In 641 the goodness of the tongue (நாநலம்) is not contained in any other goodness, which Parimelazhagar takes to mean it exceeds them all; in 982 every goodness other than the goodness of character (குணநலம்) is not counted among goodnesses at all. One chapter ranks eloquence highest for a minister, the other ranks character alone for the worthy.

641 sets the good of the tongue above every other good. 411 calls the wealth of the ear the wealth among wealths and the head of them all (செல்வத்துள் எல்லாம் தலை). The book gives the top place once to listening and once to speaking, in chapters addressed to the learner and to the minister.

642 says that since gain and ruin come from speech, one must guard against a lapse in it (காத்தோம்பல் சொல்லின்கண் சோர்வு). 127 says whatever else one fails to guard, guard the tongue (நாகாக்க), or one will grieve through a fault of speech (சொல்லிழுக்கு). The same instruction is given to the householder for his own sake and to the minister for the state's sake, as Parimelazhagar's gloss on 642 makes explicit.

642 says ruin as well as gain comes from speech and asks for vigilance against slips. 128 gives the scale of the risk: if even one harmful word has its effect (ஒன்றானும் தீச்சொல்), the good turns to no good (நன்றாகாதாகி விடும்). 128 supplies the reason why 642 treats a lapse (சோர்வு), and not only deliberate bad speech, as the danger.

Parimelazhagar reads 643 as speech that binds those who have accepted one as a friend (கேட்டார்ப் பிணிக்கும்) and makes even those who have not want friendship. 187 gives the failure of this skill: those who do not know how to make friends with pleasing talk (நகச்சொல்லி நட்பாடல் தேற்றாதவர்) part even their own kin with divisive talk. On that reading the two verses are the positive and negative of one ability, speech as what holds or breaks alliances.

On the plainer reading that Manakkudavar follows, 643 defines speech as what holds those who hear it and makes those who have not heard want to. 394 says the work of the learned is to meet so that others are glad and to part so that others think of them (உவப்பத் தலைக்கூடி உள்ளப் பிரிதல்). Both judge a person's words by the wish for more that they leave behind.

644 says to speak knowing the திறன், which Parimelazhagar takes as the relative standing of speaker and hearers. 711 gives the method: those who know the stock of words should speak after knowing the assembly and examining (அவையறிந்து ஆராய்ந்து சொல்லுக). Chapter 72 works out as a practice what 644 states as a principle.

644 asks for speech fitted to its hearers and says no virtue or gain exceeds it. 696 applies this to a single hearer, the king: know his mood, consider the time, and say what is needed in a way he will want (குறிப்பறிந்து காலம் கருதி ... வேட்பச் சொலல்). The general rule for a minister's speech becomes a specific rule for speech to power.

644 says to speak after knowing the திறன் of those concerned. 469 says that even in doing good there is error when it is done without knowing each person's character (அவரவர் பண்பறிந்து ஆற்றாக்கடை). Both make a good thing, a word or a deed, depend on fitting it to the particular person receiving it.

645 says to speak a word only after knowing that no other word can defeat it (வெல்லுஞ்சொல் இன்மை அறிந்து). 467 says to think and then commit to a task, and that saying 'we will think after committing' is a fault (எண்ணித் துணிக). Both put the testing before the irreversible step; 645 applies to an utterance the rule 467 gives for action.

646 gives a two-sided rule: speak so that others want to hear, and take the value from what others say (பிறர்சொல் பயன்கோடல்). 424 defines understanding with the same two sides: say things so they go in easily (செலச்சொல்லி) and see the subtle meaning in what comes from others' mouths (பிறர்வாய் நுண்பொருள் காண்பது). The minister's practice in 646 is what 424 calls அறிவு itself.

646 pairs speaking well with drawing the benefit from others' words. 724 sets that pair in the assembly of the learned: make what you have learned go home to them (கற்ற செலச்சொல்லி) and take what is more from those who know more (மிக்காருள் மிக்க கொளல்). 724 adds what 646 leaves open, that listening is how the speaker's own knowledge grows.

647 lists three things that make a person hard to beat in a contest: able to speak, free of lapses, unafraid (சொலல்வல்லன் சோர்விலன் அஞ்சான்). 686 defines the envoy with nearly the same set: learned, not afraid of hostile eyes (கண் அஞ்சான்), speaking so it goes home, and knowing what fits the time. The envoy chapter puts the general portrait of 647 into the one post where it is tested before an enemy.

647 says no one can easily defeat a fearless, unfaltering speaker in a contest (இகல் வெல்லல் யார்க்கும் அரிது). 872 gives the advice that follows for the other side: take on the enmity of those whose plough is the bow if you must, but not of those whose plough is the word (சொல்லேர் உழவர் பகை). Parimelazhagar takes the latter to be ministers, the people 647 describes.

648 says the world quickly takes up what is asked of it when it finds people who can speak in order and sweetly (நிரந்தினிது சொல்லுதல் வல்லார்). 387 says that for a king able to give and protect with sweet words, this world is as he sees it by his own word (தன்சொலால் தான் கண்டனைத்து). Both say the world follows pleasant speech; 387 joins giving to it, 648 orderly arrangement.

648 says the world listens readily to skilled, pleasing speakers. 1046 says the words of the poor go slack even when they speak good matter that they have understood well (நற்பொருள் நன்குணர்ந்து சொல்லினும் ... சோர்வு படும்). 1046 limits 648: how the world receives speech depends on the speaker's means as well as his skill.

649 says those who cannot say a few faultless words (மாசற்ற சில சொல்லல் தேற்றாதவர்) long to say many. 685 makes brevity the envoy's first mark: he speaks compactly (தொகச் சொல்லி), drops what is harsh, and speaks so as to please. 685 shows the positive skill whose absence 649 describes.

649 treats wanting to say many things as the sign of someone unable to say a few well. 193 says spread-out talk on useless matters (பயனில பாரித்துரைக்கும் உரை) itself announces that the speaker lacks நயன். In both, length of speech is evidence against the speaker; 193 judges his character, 649 his skill.

649 faults many words and praises a few faultless ones; the next verse faults those who cannot expound what they have learned so that others understand (உணர விரித்துரையாதார்). Manakkudavar reads the pair together: speak briefly, but also expand where it is needed. 650 keeps 649 from being taken as a rule of brevity alone.

650 likens those who cannot unfold their learning so that others grasp it to flowers that bloom in a cluster and give no scent (நாறா மலர்). 728 says the same without the image: though they have learned many things, those who cannot speak well and tellingly in a good assembly are of no use (பயமிலரே). Both hold that learning counts only when it can be communicated; Parimelazhagar's gloss on 728 gives fear as the cause, while 650 concerns the ability to explain.

Both verses use a flower's scent (நாற்றம்) for what is inside a person. In 650 the flower is fully open and gives no scent, like the learned person who cannot convey what he knows; in 1274 the scent is held inside a closed bud, like the unspoken meaning inside the girl's budding smile. The two uses mirror each other: an open display with nothing reaching others, and a closed one whose content the lover already perceives.
